Impact of COVID-19 measures on mental health, resilience and job satisfaction among healthcare professionals: A mixed-methods study

Anne E. Schramade, Malene V. van Schaik, A. H. Ayesha Lavell, and 4 more

This is a preprint; it has not been peer reviewed by a journal.

https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-9569564/v1

This work is licensed under a CC BY 4.0 License

Abstract
Background

Healthcare professionals’ mental well-being and job satisfaction was subject to severe stress during the COVID-19 pandemic. It is unclear how pandemic-related stressors, organizational and national responses, and protective factors such as support measures and nurses’ resilience, influenced psychological well-being and job satisfaction. This study aims to provide a deeper understanding of these processes.

Methods

We conducted a mixed-methods consisting of semi-structured interviews followed by a confirmatory cross-sectional survey. Seventeen nurses working in direct patient care during the pandemic participated in the qualitative phase. Interviews were analyzed thematically. Subsequently, 135 healthcare professionals, including nurses and physicians, completed a survey that was analyzed descriptively, with comparisons between professional groups.

Results

Three interconnected themes emerged: working conditions, support, and resilience. Major stressors centered on overwhelming workload, reduced professional autonomy, visitor restrictions, and resource constraints. Peer support and team cohesion emerged as the most important protective factors for well-being and job satisfaction. Post-pandemic interviews revealed discrepancies between resilience scores measured during the pandemic and nurses’ later reflections, suggesting delayed recognition of psychological strain. Compared with physicians, nurses reported disproportionate relational and enforcement burdens, particularly regarding visitor restrictions, and were less likely to view their compensation as proportional to workload. While peer support and team cohesion functioned as critical protective factors, symbolic recognition without structural improvements offered limited benefit.

Conclusion

Future healthcare crises are likely to be characterized by staff shortages, particularly among nurses. Our findings suggest that individual resilience alone is insufficient to sustain healthcare systems during prolonged crises, as frontline staff bear a substantial burden. Ensuring workforce sustainability requires systemic change, including structural investment in staffing levels, professional autonomy, and working conditions, alongside meaningful recognition and team-based support systems.

Netherlands Trial Register NL8645 (WHO ICTRP: NL-OMON56239). Registered on 23 March 2020.
